677	                        4. Discussion
678	                              The purpose of this study was to determine if there is a relationship between thermal
679	                        asymmetries provided by thermography and performance in a repeated sprint ability (RSA)
680	                        test and in countermovement jumps (CMJs) before and after the RSA test. The results of the
681	                        RSA test showed a significant interaction between hamstring asymmetry and the number
682	                        of sprints in the RSAt and in the % Diff. The hamstring high-asymmetry group showed a
683	                        higher %Diff in sprint 2, which means that there is a significative longer time with respect
684	 Sensors 2023, 23, 631                                                                                            7 of 9
685	
686	
687	
688	
689	                        to sprint 1 (worse performance) than in the low-asymmetry group. On the other hand,
690	                        the hamstring low-asymmetry group reported a higher %Best in sprints 2, 3 and 4. The
691	                        cause of this difference in the hamstring %Best may be attributable to the fact that the
692	                        low-asymmetry group had the best sprint, which was very fast; therefore, the following best
693	                        ones have a significant difference (worse). On the other hand, no differences were found in
694	                        the thigh and calf groups for any variable. The reason why the only thermal asymmetry that
695	                        influenced the performance was that of hamstrings could be their importance in sprinting,
696	                        as they play a crucial role in generating force in the propulsive part of the sprint [28]
697	                        and are clearly the most frequently injured muscle during sprinting [4]. The majority of
698	                        hamstring muscle injuries occur while the athlete is running at maximal or close to maximal
699	                        speeds [29] Many investigations have measured hamstring activity during sprinting with
700	                        electromyographic (EMG), and found that the hamstrings are active from the middle of
701	                        the swing to the final stance Some of these studies have reported that peak activity occurs
702	                        during terminal swing [30], whereas others have found it to occur during stance [31]. Proof
703	                        of the effort that these muscles exert in the sprint is that an increase in running speed of
704	                        80–100% is linked with an increase in net hamstring muscle force and energy absorption of
705	                        1.4 and 1.9 times, respectively [32]. However, this study took data from athletes running on
706	                        a treadmill, and the mechanical properties of treadmill surfaces are different from those
707	                        of the surfaces on which the athletes usually train and compete (e.g., artificial turf or an
708	                        athletic track) [33]. This factor may influence running anatomy, so the results should be
709	                        interpreted with caution.
710	                              Regarding the CMJ results, the low thermal asymmetry hamstring group has signif-
711	                        icantly higher values in the CMJ post-RSA, while in the calf and thigh groups, there are
712	                        no significant differences in either CMJ pre- or CMJ post-RSA. Thus, the high thermal
713	                        asymmetry hamstring group’s performance was similar to that of the low thermal asym-
714	                        metry hamstring group before the RSA, and then its performance decreased in the CMJ
715	                        post-RSA. This can be indicative of fatigue, as a decreased average CMJ jump height can
716	                        indicate neuromuscular fatigue [34]. The reason why significant differences are only found
717	                        in the high-asymmetry hamstring group (and not in the calf and thigh groups) may be that
718	                        hamstrings are the most implicated and frequently injured group in sprinting [28], while
719	                        calves and thighs seem to play a less crucial role in sprinting; therefore, asymmetry takes
720	                        longer to turn into fatigue when performing an RSA test, as they are less implicated in
721	                        this activity.
722	                              Although the results of this study seem to provide evidence in terms of using and
723	                        interpreting thermography to assess RSA and CMJ performance in elite football players,
724	                        the results must be interpreted with caution, as certain limitations should be considered.
725	                        First, thermography was carried out in just one session; applying thermography in a higher
726	                        number of sessions would allow us to corroborate the results of the study. Second, a low
727	                        asymmetry cut point was established, and settling a higher asymmetry cut point would
728	                        probably show stronger correlations. Finally, the sample was very small, so future research
729	                        should be carried out to look for evidence and to check whether these results apply to
730	                        different genders, ages and competitive levels.
731	                              From a practical point of view, if football coaches can access the thermographs of their
732	                        players, they should focus especially on hamstrings (rather than calves and thighs) and
733	                        modify the training if necessary. These muscles appear to be the ones with more influence
734	                        on the test results, as they are the only ones for which thermal asymmetry of over 0.2 ◦ C
735	                        had an effect.
736	
737	                        5. Conclusions
738	                             Thermography can provide information about performance in CMJ and RSA tests for
739	                        hamstring asymmetries over 0.2 ◦ C; meanwhile, calf and thigh asymmetries over 0.2 ◦ C do
740	                        not seem to have a relationship with performance in these tests. In short, thermography
741	                        results have some correlation with CMJ and RSA performance, but stablishing higher cut
742	                        off points would probably allow us to find stronger correlations for hamstring asymmetries,

                                         Abstract: Football is a very demanding sport which requires players to exert maximum effort,
                                         producing fatigue and eventually injuries. Thermography can be used to detect fatigue and prevent
                                         its consequences through thermal asymmetries in the bilateral body areas; however, its adequacy for
                                         elite footballers has not been widely studied. Therefore, the objective of the present investigation
                                         was to determine the suitability of thermography to detect fatigue in male football players. For
                                         this reason, twenty participants were gathered into a pair of subgroups (low [<0.2 ◦ C] vs. high
                                         thermal asymmetry [≥0.2 ◦ C]) based on a thermography session of the lower limbs (thighs, calves,
                                         and hamstrings). After the thermography session, players performed CMJs before and after an
                                         RSA test (6 × 30 m/2000 ). A mixed two-way analysis of variance and Bonferroni post hoc pairwise
                                         comparisons were undertaken to analyse the results. No significant differences (p > 0.05) were found
                                         in any of the RSA test variables between low and high thermal asymmetry groups for thighs and

                        progress, prevent overtraining, decrease injury risk and improve performance [7]. However,
                        very few studies have actively investigated how to measure fatigue and adjust training
                        accordingly.
                              Fatigue can be measured through internal and external loads [5]. In football, there are
                        several internal load methods that are very popular to measure fatigue and response to
                        exercise; however, most of them present some disadvantages, so they should be combined
                        with other methods. Heart rate measurements are the most common, but they are imprecise
                        in high-intensity actions and sprints, which are crucial aspects of football [8]. Blood and
                        bone markers are more precise, but they are difficult to extract on a weekly basis (price
                        and time), and some players can feel uncomfortable being exposed continuously to them.
                        Therefore, extracting them whenever the physical status of the player needs to be known
                        can be unsustainable during regular-season training [9]. Questionnaires are very simple to
                        administer but particularly subjective, introducing a high risk of bias [10].
                              Conversely, there are some physical tests that can help to check the current physical
                        condition of the athletes through external loads. It has been evidenced that velocity loss
                        is a reliable marker of neuromuscular fatigue, which is described as a decrease in the
                        physical and mental functions [11]. This is why most of the scientific literature has used
                        the repeated sprint ability (RSA) test to measure fatigue, especially in team sports such as
                        football; this is because RSA and the ability to exercise at high intensity are key capacities
                        for optimal performance, and a decreased sprint repetition capacity is a good indicator
                        of fatigue in sports [12]. However, this method can lack precision in some situations, as
                        the scientific literature has found that sprint performance can be maintained in situations
                        of neuromuscular fatigue after match play [13]. This is why some coaches incorporate a
                        stretching–shortening movement, such as a countermovement jump (CMJ) to detect fatigue,
                        as it can highlight impairments in jump performance between two events [14]; a good
                        relationship between sprint ability and CMJ capacity has been verified [14].
                              Therefore, scientific evidence has shown CMJ performance to be an objective marker
                        of fatigue and supercompensation, as neuromuscular fatigue has been associated with a
                        decrease in the average CMJ height [15], causing this method to be used frequently to assess
                        neuromuscular fatigue [16]. However, when using RSA to assess neuromuscular fatigue,
                        the number of sprints induces great variability between athletes [17]. In addition, when
                        using CMJs, it is important to consider that the same fatiguing stimuli can elicit different
                        effects between individuals, and sometimes athletes can adjust their jumping strategy
                        to maintain their performance [18]. Moreover, players’ need to exert maximal effort to
                        measure fatigue is not optimal, as this effort increases injury risk. Hence, the use of other
                        technologies which can provide information and help coaches without the need to perform
                        a physical test, can be considered. In this sense, one option is infrared thermography (IRT),
                        which is a non-radiating, contact-free, safe and non-invasive technology that monitors
                        physiological variables through the control of the skin temperature [19].
                              This technology gauges the correlation between muscle activation and skin tempera-
                        ture, as muscle and skin temperature are directly correlated. The information this technol-
                        ogy provided is based on the hyperthermic and hypothermic responses of the skin [20], due
                        to the fact that thermography is a reliable method to assess skin temperature [21]. Moreover,
                        athletes are presumed to keep their thermal pattern constant in baseline conditions, and
                        thermal asymmetries in the bilateral body areas (e.g., ankle, knee, hamstring or elbow) are
                        linked to factors related to injuries, such as inflammation or secondary trauma, as in normal
                        conditions, the temperature of both sides of the bilateral areas should increase equally [22].
                        IRT can detect these asymmetries by comparing bilateral body areas, showing potential in-
                        jury risk due to incorrect work assimilations provoked by factors such as excessive training,
                        poor technique or muscle overload [23].
                              The relevance of IRT is that it can detect temperature asymmetries (and consequent
                        risks) before other markers such as pain, making this method extraordinarily effective and
                        applicable in preventing injuries [23]. If IRT provides coaches with the ability to detect
                        impairments in bilateral body areas before pain, it can allow them to modify the training

                                        Players completed 2 CMJ tests: (1) after warming up and (2) after the RSA test, with

                        jump performance. Each player performed three jumps before and after the RSA test (with
                        2 min of recovery between jumps). The average of the three jumps was calculated for the
                        statistical analysis.

                        2.4.3. Repeated Sprint Ability (RSA)
                              The RSA test included six sprints of 30 m with 20 s recovery between sprints. Two
                        pairs of photocells (Witty, Microgate, Bolzano, Italy), placed at 0 and 30 m, were used. The
                        following measures were calculated: sprint time (RSAt), best sprint time, average time,
                        total time, percentage difference between the first and the rest of the sprints during the RSA
                        test − %Diff − [((sprint time − first sprint time)/first sprint time) × 100] and percentage
                        difference between the best and the rest of the sprints during the RSA test − %Best −
                        [((sprint time − best time)/best time) × 100]. The previous two sprints performed during
                        the warm-up were used as a control measure to ensure that players performed the RSA test
                        at maximum speed. If the time of the first RSA test sprint was longer (>5%) than the best
                        individual sprint performed before the start of the test, the RSA test was not considered
                        valid, and the player had to repeat the test after 5 min of recovery.

                        2.5. Statistical Analysis
                             The data are presented as means ± standard deviations. The normal distribution of
                        the variables was confirmed by histogram charts and the Shapiro–Wilk distribution test.
                        A mixed two-way analysis of variance was performed to analyse the effect of the level of
                        thermal asymmetry on the RSA variables depending on the sprint number. The thermal
                        asymmetry group was used as an independent factor, and the sprint number as a repeated
                        measured factor to control the interaction of the thermal asymmetry group with the sprint
                        progression. Bonferroni post hoc pairwise comparisons were undertaken to compare the
                        RSA variables of the two groups of thermal asymmetries in each of the sprints, including
                        the confidence interval (95%). The effect size (ES) was calculated for all the inference
                        tests using the partial eta squared (ηp2 = ES) value with the following interpretation:
                        small (ES = 0.01–0.059); medium (ES = 0.06–0.14); and large effects (ES > 0.14). The level of
                        significance was set at p < 0.05 for all the tests, and all the data were statistically analysed
                        using SPSS V24.0. (IBM Corp. Released 2016. IBM SPSS Statistics for Windows, Version
                        24.0. Armonk, NY: IBM Corp.)

                        4. Discussion
                              The purpose of this study was to determine if there is a relationship between thermal
                        asymmetries provided by thermography and performance in a repeated sprint ability (RSA)
                        test and in countermovement jumps (CMJs) before and after the RSA test. The results of the
                        RSA test showed a significant interaction between hamstring asymmetry and the number
                        of sprints in the RSAt and in the % Diff. The hamstring high-asymmetry group showed a
                        higher %Diff in sprint 2, which means that there is a significative longer time with respect
 Sensors 2023, 23, 631                                                                                            7 of 9




                        to sprint 1 (worse performance) than in the low-asymmetry group. On the other hand,
                        the hamstring low-asymmetry group reported a higher %Best in sprints 2, 3 and 4. The
                        cause of this difference in the hamstring %Best may be attributable to the fact that the
                        low-asymmetry group had the best sprint, which was very fast; therefore, the following best
                        ones have a significant difference (worse). On the other hand, no differences were found in
                        the thigh and calf groups for any variable. The reason why the only thermal asymmetry that
                        influenced the performance was that of hamstrings could be their importance in sprinting,
                        as they play a crucial role in generating force in the propulsive part of the sprint [28]
                        and are clearly the most frequently injured muscle during sprinting [4]. The majority of
                        hamstring muscle injuries occur while the athlete is running at maximal or close to maximal
                        speeds [29] Many investigations have measured hamstring activity during sprinting with
                        electromyographic (EMG), and found that the hamstrings are active from the middle of
                        the swing to the final stance Some of these studies have reported that peak activity occurs
                        during terminal swing [30], whereas others have found it to occur during stance [31]. Proof
                        of the effort that these muscles exert in the sprint is that an increase in running speed of
                        80–100% is linked with an increase in net hamstring muscle force and energy absorption of
                        1.4 and 1.9 times, respectively [32]. However, this study took data from athletes running on
                        a treadmill, and the mechanical properties of treadmill surfaces are different from those
                        of the surfaces on which the athletes usually train and compete (e.g., artificial turf or an
                        athletic track) [33]. This factor may influence running anatomy, so the results should be
                        interpreted with caution.
                              Regarding the CMJ results, the low thermal asymmetry hamstring group has signif-
                        icantly higher values in the CMJ post-RSA, while in the calf and thigh groups, there are
                        no significant differences in either CMJ pre- or CMJ post-RSA. Thus, the high thermal
                        asymmetry hamstring group’s performance was similar to that of the low thermal asym-
                        metry hamstring group before the RSA, and then its performance decreased in the CMJ
                        post-RSA. This can be indicative of fatigue, as a decreased average CMJ jump height can
                        indicate neuromuscular fatigue [34]. The reason why significant differences are only found
                        in the high-asymmetry hamstring group (and not in the calf and thigh groups) may be that
                        hamstrings are the most implicated and frequently injured group in sprinting [28], while
                        calves and thighs seem to play a less crucial role in sprinting; therefore, asymmetry takes
                        longer to turn into fatigue when performing an RSA test, as they are less implicated in
                        this activity.
                              Although the results of this study seem to provide evidence in terms of using and
                        interpreting thermography to assess RSA and CMJ performance in elite football players,
                        the results must be interpreted with caution, as certain limitations should be considered.
                        First, thermography was carried out in just one session; applying thermography in a higher
                        number of sessions would allow us to corroborate the results of the study. Second, a low
                        asymmetry cut point was established, and settling a higher asymmetry cut point would
                        probably show stronger correlations. Finally, the sample was very small, so future research
                        should be carried out to look for evidence and to check whether these results apply to
                        different genders, ages and competitive levels.
                              From a practical point of view, if football coaches can access the thermographs of their
                        players, they should focus especially on hamstrings (rather than calves and thighs) and
                        modify the training if necessary. These muscles appear to be the ones with more influence
                        on the test results, as they are the only ones for which thermal asymmetry of over 0.2 ◦ C
                        had an effect.

                        5. Conclusions
                             Thermography can provide information about performance in CMJ and RSA tests for
                        hamstring asymmetries over 0.2 ◦ C; meanwhile, calf and thigh asymmetries over 0.2 ◦ C do
                        not seem to have a relationship with performance in these tests. In short, thermography
                        results have some correlation with CMJ and RSA performance, but stablishing higher cut
                        off points would probably allow us to find stronger correlations for hamstring asymmetries,

                                   and maybe some correlation for calf and thigh asymmetries which would be helpful for
                                   coaches and athletes.

22	Abstract
23	Elite soccer players consistently report using several recovery methods after practices and games. However, it is unclear how
24	their subsequent performance could be enhanced using broad protocols. The aim of this study was to compare the effectiveness
25	of two different comprehensive recovery protocols in physiological, neuromuscular, and perceptual outcomes. Eighteen Mexican
26	National Team players (19.56 ± 0.62 years) were recruited. Using a randomized parallel group design, players followed one of
27	two recovery protocols: (a) carbohydrate and protein shake, foam roller, cold-water immersion, and tart cherry juice concen-
28	trate (n = 9) or (b) carbohydrate and protein shake, stretching, and intermittent cold-water immersion (n = 9) following the
29	completion of an unofﬁcial game and the day after. Muscular creatine kinase, countermovement jump, hamstring maximal vol-
30	untary contraction, perceived recovery, and muscle soreness were assessed before, immediately after, and 20-44-68 h post-
31	game. Signiﬁcant effects (set at ρ≤0.05) of time were present in both interventions. Muscular creatine kinase was normalized
32	entirely at 68 h post-game, while neuromuscular and perceptual outcomes were homogenized at 44 h. No statistically signiﬁcant
33	effects between protocols were found. Still, the interaction effects showed changes only in the group using protocol (a) at post-
34	game and 20 h after in neuromuscular and muscle soreness. There were large correlations between muscular creatine kinase
35	and accelerations, decelerations, sprints, and high-speed running distances. In conclusion, the interventions are equally effective
36	for improving physiological, neuromuscular, and perceptual outcomes. Thus, elite soccer players may beneﬁt from different com-

Abstract
Elite soccer players consistently report using several recovery methods after practices and games. However, it is unclear how
their subsequent performance could be enhanced using broad protocols. The aim of this study was to compare the effectiveness
of two different comprehensive recovery protocols in physiological, neuromuscular, and perceptual outcomes. Eighteen Mexican
National Team players (19.56 ± 0.62 years) were recruited. Using a randomized parallel group design, players followed one of
two recovery protocols: (a) carbohydrate and protein shake, foam roller, cold-water immersion, and tart cherry juice concen-
trate (n = 9) or (b) carbohydrate and protein shake, stretching, and intermittent cold-water immersion (n = 9) following the
completion of an unofﬁcial game and the day after. Muscular creatine kinase, countermovement jump, hamstring maximal vol-
untary contraction, perceived recovery, and muscle soreness were assessed before, immediately after, and 20-44-68 h post-
game. Signiﬁcant effects (set at ρ≤0.05) of time were present in both interventions. Muscular creatine kinase was normalized
entirely at 68 h post-game, while neuromuscular and perceptual outcomes were homogenized at 44 h. No statistically signiﬁcant
effects between protocols were found. Still, the interaction effects showed changes only in the group using protocol (a) at post-
game and 20 h after in neuromuscular and muscle soreness. There were large correlations between muscular creatine kinase
and accelerations, decelerations, sprints, and high-speed running distances. In conclusion, the interventions are equally effective
for improving physiological, neuromuscular, and perceptual outcomes. Thus, elite soccer players may beneﬁt from different com-
binations of methods after practices or games to obtain positive effects on recovery after them.

13	      Context: Professional soccer players who have sustained a lower limb injury are up to 3× more likely to suffer a reinjury, often of
14	      increased severity. Previous injury has been shown to induce compensatory strategies during neuromuscular screening tests,
15	      which might mask deﬁcits and lead to misinterpretation of readiness to play based on task outcome measures. Objective: To
16	      investigate the inﬂuence of previous injury in professional soccer players on countermovement jump (CMJ) performance and
17	      movement strategy. Design: Cross-sectional. Setting: Professional soccer club competing in the English Championship (tier 2).
18	      Patients (or Other Participants): Outﬁeld players with a minimum of 6 years as a professional. Intervention(s): Players were
19	      categorized as previously injured (n = 10) or not injured (n = 10). All players completed double- and single-leg CMJ trials. Main
20	      Outcome Measures: CMJ performance was quantiﬁed as jump height and ﬂight time:contraction time ratio. CMJ movement
21	      strategy was quantiﬁed as force–time history, differentiating eccentric and concentric phases and CMJ depth. Results: Double-
22	      leg CMJ was not sensitive to previous injury in performance or movement strategy. In contrast, single-leg CMJ performance was
23	      impaired in players with previous injury, who generated signiﬁcantly lower eccentric and concentric peak force and rate of force
24	      development, and a deeper countermovement. Impaired single-leg CMJ performance was also evident in the nonaffected limb of
25	      previously injured players, suggesting cross-contamination. Hierarchical ordering revealed that the eccentric phase of the CMJ
26	      contributed little to performance in previously injured players. In noninjured players, the eccentric rate of force development and
27	      concentric peak force were able to account for up to 89% of the variation in CMJ performance. Conclusions: Single-leg CMJ is
28	      advocated for player proﬁling, being more sensitive to previous injury, and negating the opportunity for interlimb compensation
29	      strategies. Movement strategy deﬁcits in previously injured players suggest rehabilitation foci speciﬁc to eccentric force
30	      development.

         The Inﬂuence of Injury History on Countermovement Jump
        Performance and Movement Strategy in Professional Soccer
          Players: Implications for Proﬁling and Rehabilitation Foci
                                             Andy Mitchell, Craig Holding, and Matt Greig

      Context: Professional soccer players who have sustained a lower limb injury are up to 3× more likely to suffer a reinjury, often of
      increased severity. Previous injury has been shown to induce compensatory strategies during neuromuscular screening tests,
      which might mask deﬁcits and lead to misinterpretation of readiness to play based on task outcome measures. Objective: To
      investigate the inﬂuence of previous injury in professional soccer players on countermovement jump (CMJ) performance and
      movement strategy. Design: Cross-sectional. Setting: Professional soccer club competing in the English Championship (tier 2).
      Patients (or Other Participants): Outﬁeld players with a minimum of 6 years as a professional. Intervention(s): Players were
      categorized as previously injured (n = 10) or not injured (n = 10). All players completed double- and single-leg CMJ trials. Main
      Outcome Measures: CMJ performance was quantiﬁed as jump height and ﬂight time:contraction time ratio. CMJ movement
      strategy was quantiﬁed as force–time history, differentiating eccentric and concentric phases and CMJ depth. Results: Double-
      leg CMJ was not sensitive to previous injury in performance or movement strategy. In contrast, single-leg CMJ performance was
      impaired in players with previous injury, who generated signiﬁcantly lower eccentric and concentric peak force and rate of force
      development, and a deeper countermovement. Impaired single-leg CMJ performance was also evident in the nonaffected limb of
      previously injured players, suggesting cross-contamination. Hierarchical ordering revealed that the eccentric phase of the CMJ
      contributed little to performance in previously injured players. In noninjured players, the eccentric rate of force development and
      concentric peak force were able to account for up to 89% of the variation in CMJ performance. Conclusions: Single-leg CMJ is
      advocated for player proﬁling, being more sensitive to previous injury, and negating the opportunity for interlimb compensation
      strategies. Movement strategy deﬁcits in previously injured players suggest rehabilitation foci speciﬁc to eccentric force
      development.

      Keywords: elite male soccer, neuromuscular performance, player proﬁling, previous injury

17	                                       Paul M. Inclan, MD,† Andrew W. Kuhn, MD,† Peter S. Chang, MD,†‡ Christina Mack, PhD,§

21	                                       Context: Numerous researchers have leveraged publicly available internet sources to publish clinical research concerning
22	                                       incidence and recovery from injuries in National Football League (NFL) players.
23	                                       Objective: This study aims to (1) provide a comprehensive systematic review of all publicly obtained data studies (PODS)
24	                                       regarding concussions in NFL athletes and (2) quantify the percentage of injuries identified by these studies in comparison
25	                                       with published concussion data from the NFL injury database.
26	                                       Study Selection: A systematic review was conducted in accordance with PRISMA guidelines to identify all published
27	                                       studies utilizing publicly obtained data regarding concussions in NFL athletes.
28	                                       Study Design: Systematic review.
29	                                       Level of Evidence: Level 4.
30	                                       Data Extraction: Manuscript details, factors related to the athletes of interest (eg, study period, positions included), and
31	                                       results (eg, concussion rate, number of total concussions, return-to-play data) were extracted independently by 2 authors.
32	                                       Results were compared with incident concussions reported from 2015 to 2019 by each medical staff member to the NFL
33	                                       database linked to the League’s electronic health record (EHR).
34	                                       Results: A total of 20 concussion-focused manuscripts based on PODS were identified from 2014 to 2020. PODS captured
35	                                       between 20% and 90% of concussions (mean, 70%) reported by medical staff to the injury database. PODS reported that
36	                                       55% of concussions occurred on offensive plays, 45% on defensive plays and <1% occurred during special teams plays,
37	                                       compared with 44%, 37%, and 18%, respectively, as indicated by published data from the NFL injury database. When
38	                                       analyzed by position groups, running backs and quarterbacks comprised the most over-represented positions concussed in
39	                                       PODS, while offensive linemen, defensive backs, and linebackers comprised the most under-represented positions.
40	                                       Conclusion: PODS captured approximately 70% of concussions reported by NFL medical staff to the NFL injury database.
41	                                       There is heterogeneity in the degree to which PODS were able to identify concussions, with a bias toward concussions
42	                                       among players at higher profile positions.
43	                                       Keywords: concussion; epidemiology; National Football League; team sports

                                       Validity of Research Based on Publicly
                                       Obtained Data in Sports Medicine: A
                                       Quantitative Assessment of Concussions
                                       in the National Football League
                                       Paul M. Inclan, MD,† Andrew W. Kuhn, MD,† Peter S. Chang, MD,†‡ Christina Mack, PhD,§
                                       Gary S. Solomon, PhD,||¶ Allen K. Sills, MD,||¶ and Matthew J. Matava, MD*†


                                       Context: Numerous researchers have leveraged publicly available internet sources to publish clinical research concerning
                                       incidence and recovery from injuries in National Football League (NFL) players.
                                       Objective: This study aims to (1) provide a comprehensive systematic review of all publicly obtained data studies (PODS)
                                       regarding concussions in NFL athletes and (2) quantify the percentage of injuries identified by these studies in comparison
                                       with published concussion data from the NFL injury database.
                                       Study Selection: A systematic review was conducted in accordance with PRISMA guidelines to identify all published
                                       studies utilizing publicly obtained data regarding concussions in NFL athletes.
                                       Study Design: Systematic review.
                                       Level of Evidence: Level 4.
                                       Data Extraction: Manuscript details, factors related to the athletes of interest (eg, study period, positions included), and
                                       results (eg, concussion rate, number of total concussions, return-to-play data) were extracted independently by 2 authors.
                                       Results were compared with incident concussions reported from 2015 to 2019 by each medical staff member to the NFL
                                       database linked to the League’s electronic health record (EHR).
                                       Results: A total of 20 concussion-focused manuscripts based on PODS were identified from 2014 to 2020. PODS captured
                                       between 20% and 90% of concussions (mean, 70%) reported by medical staff to the injury database. PODS reported that
                                       55% of concussions occurred on offensive plays, 45% on defensive plays and <1% occurred during special teams plays,
                                       compared with 44%, 37%, and 18%, respectively, as indicated by published data from the NFL injury database. When
                                       analyzed by position groups, running backs and quarterbacks comprised the most over-represented positions concussed in
                                       PODS, while offensive linemen, defensive backs, and linebackers comprised the most under-represented positions.
                                       Conclusion: PODS captured approximately 70% of concussions reported by NFL medical staff to the NFL injury database.
                                       There is heterogeneity in the degree to which PODS were able to identify concussions, with a bias toward concussions
                                       among players at higher profile positions.
                                       Keywords: concussion; epidemiology; National Football League; team sports

 "primaryDomain": "Brain Health & Psychology",
 "domains": ["Brain Health & Psychology", "Athlete Wellbeing", "Sports Medicine & Injury"],
 "audiences": ["Sports Medicine", "Athletic Training", "Research & Analytics"],
 "sports": ["American Football"],
 "populations": ["Professional / Elite"],
 "evidenceSummary": "Cross-sectional online and paper survey of 1,784 former NFL players (mean age 52.3 years, 86.9% with at least one lifetime concussion). Each one-year-later start to organized football was linked to small, significant differences in PROMIS anxiety, depression, sleep disturbance, pain interference and emotional-behavioral dyscontrol scores (B of about -0.16 to -0.22 per year), but not to cognitive or physical function. Starting age was not associated with self-reported anxiety, depression, dementia or mild cognitive impairment, while age group was strongly associated with these diagnoses and with all outcomes.",
 "screeningLimitations": "Self-reported data from a voluntary sample of retired players, with recall and ascertainment bias, and a cross-sectional design that cannot show cause. The Conclusions state an association with cognitive and physical function, but the Results and Table 2 show no significant main effect for either (p = 0.116 and 0.860); this review follows the Results and Table 2.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff may read the link between a younger starting age and higher anxiety or depression scores as proof that early tackle play causes later mood problems, when the associations are small and cross-sectional.",
 "paper": {
  "year": 2022,
  "citation": "Lempke LB, Walton SR, Brett BL, Chandran A, DeFreese JD, Mannix R, et al. Relating American Football Age of First Exposure to Patient-Reported Outcomes and Medical Diagnoses Among Former National Football League Players: An NFL-LONG Study. Sports Medicine. 2022.",
  "doi": "10.1007/s40279-022-01795-9",
  "abstract": "A cross-sectional survey of 1,784 former NFL players asked whether the age at which they first played organized football was linked to self-reported function and medical diagnoses, and whether that link changed with current age. Earlier starting age was linked to slightly lower mood, sleep, pain and behavior scores, but not to diagnoses, and no age interaction was found.",
  "tldr": "Among former NFL players, starting football earlier was linked only to small differences in some self-reported mood, sleep and pain scores. It was not linked to dementia, mild cognitive impairment, anxiety or depression diagnoses, and current age mattered much more.",
  "methods": "Former NFL players completed a general health questionnaire online or on paper, covering age, age of first exposure to football, self-reported diagnoses, and PROMIS and Neuro-QOL measures. Multivariable linear and Poisson regression models tested starting age, age group and their interaction, with the interaction dropped when it was not significant.",
  "findings": "Each one-year delay in starting football was linked to a 0.16 to 0.22 point lower PROMIS T-score for anxiety, depression, sleep disturbance, pain interference and emotional-behavioral dyscontrol, with no link to cognitive or physical function. Starting age was not associated with any diagnosis (prevalence ratios 0.99 to 1.02 per year, p of 0.449 or higher), while dementia and mild cognitive impairment were much more common in the older age groups. No starting age by age interaction was significant.",
  "limitations": "Self-reported data, voluntary participation and a cross-sectional design limit causal inference, and effect sizes were small (R2 0.03 to 0.06). Concussion history and total years of play were deliberately not adjusted for, and the Conclusions claim an association with cognitive and physical function that the Results and Table 2 do not support.",
  "practicalImplications": "Starting age appears to be a minor factor in later mood, sleep and pain scores compared with current age in this group. Clinicians should not treat early starting age as a strong predictor of later mood or cognitive problems, and should focus on factors the authors call modifiable, such as exercise, diet and sleep.",
  "athleteDev": "This is a long-term health study of retired players, so it does not measure athlete performance. It offers only weak evidence that an earlier start to tackle football has a small effect on later self-reported mood and sleep, which is background for youth decisions rather than a basis for them.",
  "rtp": "This study covers retired players and does not look at return to sport, so it cannot be used to decide when an athlete can return after a concussion or other injury."
 }
}

Players were grouped as low (under 0.2 deg C) or high (0.2 deg C or more) thermal asymmetry for each muscle group.   "doi": "10.3390/s23020631",
  "abstract": "The authors tested whether lower-limb skin temperature asymmetry measured by thermography related to repeated sprint performance and countermovement jump height in 20 male professional football players. Only hamstring asymmetry showed a relationship with sprint and jump results, and thigh and calf asymmetry did not.",
  "tldr": "Hamstring temperature asymmetry showed a few links to sprint and jump results in 20 professional players, but the findings are preliminary. Do not use thermography alone to plan training loads.",
  "methods": "Cross-sectional study with one thermography session of the thighs, calves and hamstrings after 48 hours of rest, followed by a countermovement jump, a 6 x 30 m repeated sprint test with 20 seconds of recovery between sprints, and a second jump. Players were grouped by asymmetry (0.2 deg C cut-off) for each muscle and compared with mixed two-way ANOVA and Bonferroni post hoc tests.",
  "findings": "Thigh and calf asymmetry had no significant effect on any sprint variable. For hamstrings, asymmetry affected the best-sprint percentage difference (F = 6.59, p = 0.018), and the high-asymmetry group had a larger percentage slowdown at sprint 2 (p = 0.013). Post-test jump height was higher in the low-asymmetry hamstring group (37.2 vs 32.8 cm, p = 0.013), with no difference before the sprint test.",
  "limitations": "The sample is small (20 players), the testing was done once, and the 0.2 deg C cut-off was chosen for practical reasons. The abstract's description of the first-sprint result does not match the Results, and the authors do not test a mechanism for the counter-intuitive direction of some hamstring effects.",
  "practicalImplications": "Coaches with access to thermal images could note hamstring asymmetry above 0.2 deg C alongside other monitoring data. The study does not show that changing training because of asymmetry improves sprinting or jumping, and the authors themselves call for replication.",
  "athleteDev": "The paper hints that hamstring temperature asymmetry may relate to jump height after repeated sprints, which could prompt a closer look at fatigue. The effects are small, the sample is small and some sprint results run against expectation, so treat it as a prompt to investigate rather than a performance tool.",
  "rtp": "The players were healthy and free of recent injury or pain, so the study cannot show whether thermal asymmetry signals injury risk or readiness after injury. It should not be used in return-to-sport decisions."
 }

{
 "id": "Q19",
 "sourceFile": "Risk factors for hamstring muscle injury in male elite football - Medical expert experience and conclusions from 15 European Champions League clubs.pdf",
 "decision": "INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason": "",
 "degradedReason": "",
 "doiMissing": false,
 "identityCheck": "Title in the text (Risk factors for hamstring muscle injury in male elite football: medical expert experience and conclusions from 15 European Champions League clubs) matches the filename.",
 "confidence": "medium",
 "studyDesign": "Cross-sectional Study",
 "primaryDomain": "Sports Medicine & Injury",
 "domains": ["Sports Medicine & Injury", "Training & Performance"],
 "audiences": ["Sports Medicine", "Athletic Training", "Coaching", "Performance"],
 "sports": ["Soccer"],
 "populations": ["Professional / Elite", "Male Athletes"],
 "evidenceSummary": "Expert-opinion survey of chief medical officers from 15 European male professional clubs, with each club's hamstring injury burden over 2019/20 and 2020/21 used to split the clubs into 7 lower-burden and 8 higher-burden groups. Respondents suggested 21 modifiable hamstring risk factors and rated each on a 5-point importance scale. The top-rated factors were poor communication between medical and coaching staff (weighted average 3.7) and lack of regular high-speed training (3.6), and the higher-burden group rated coach leadership style, fatigue and player wellness as more important.",
 "screeningLimitations": "The findings are the perceived views of 15 medical officers rather than measured player-level or causal evidence, and the sample is small with only two seasons of injury data. The authors call the design an observational cohort study, but the risk-factor ratings come from a single survey, so it is coded as cross-sectional.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could read the ranking as proof that coaching style and communication cause hamstring injuries, when these are expert opinions from 15 clubs with no causal testing.",
 "paper": {
  "year": 2023,
  "citation": "Ekstrand J, Ueblacker P, Van Zoest W, Verheijen R, Vanhecke B, van Wijk M, et al. Risk factors for hamstring muscle injury in male elite football: medical expert experience and conclusions from 15 European Champions League clubs. BMJ Open Sport & Exercise Medicine. 2023;9:e001461.",
  "doi": "10.1136/bmjsem-2022-001461",
  "abstract": "Chief medical officers from 15 European professional clubs suggested and rated risk factors for hamstring injury, and their views were compared between clubs with lower and higher than average hamstring injury burden. Most of the 21 factors identified were extrinsic (coaching, team or club), led by poor communication between medical and coaching staff.",
  "tldr": "Club medical leaders mostly point to coaching, team and club factors, rather than player factors, as preventable causes of hamstring injury. Communication between medical and coaching staff and lack of high-speed training rank highest.",
  "methods": "Observational study in 15 clubs from the UEFA Elite Club Injury Study. Each club's chief medical officer answered an open question on preventable hamstring risk factors, then rated each of 21 factors on a 5-point importance scale. Clubs were divided by whether their hamstring injury burden was below or above the average across 2019/20 and 2020/21, and ratings were compared between the two groups.",
  "findings": "Lack of communication between medical and coaching staff had the highest weighted average (3.7), followed by lack of regular high-speed exposure in training (3.6). Of the 21 factors, 12 were extrinsic and 9 intrinsic, with mean importance 3.1 and 2.9. The higher-burden group rated coach leadership style much higher (3.3 vs 2.1), and rated fatigue (3.6 vs 2.6) and player wellness (3.0 vs 2.0) higher, while the lower-burden group rated lack of high-speed training higher (3.8 vs 3.5).",
  "limitations": "This is an opinion-based survey of 15 clubs with small groups (7 and 8) and two seasons of injury data, so causation cannot be inferred and the results may not generalize. Hamstring injuries were grouped regardless of type or mechanism, and players were not asked for their views. The authors call the design a cohort study, but the core data are a one-time survey.",
  "practicalImplications": "Clubs could review how medical and coaching staff communicate about prevention, load and rehabilitation, since that was the most highly rated factor. The paper also points to training load, high-speed exposure and fatigue as things coaches control. These are the respondents' views rather than proven interventions, so clubs should track hamstring injuries in their own squad.",
  "athleteDev": "The paper names high-speed training exposure and load management as factors that performance and coaching staff control, so they are sensible areas to review with coaches. The lower-burden clubs rated lack of regular high-speed football as the top technical factor, but the ratings are opinions rather than tested effects.",
  "rtp": "Residual weakness after a previous hamstring injury was rated among the most important factors for individual players, and the authors note that incomplete strength and speed rehabilitation raises re-injury risk. The study tests no rehabilitation protocol and cannot set return-to-play criteria."
 }
}

 "sourceFile": "The effectiveness of two comprehensive recovery protocols on performance and physiological measures in elite soccer players - A parallel group-randomized trial.pdf",
 "decision": "INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason": "",
 "degradedReason": "",
 "doiMissing": false,
 "identityCheck": "Title in the text (The effectiveness of two comprehensive recovery protocols on performance and physiological measures in elite soccer players: A parallel group-randomized trial) matches the filename.",
 "confidence": "high",
 "studyDesign": "Randomized Controlled Trial",
 "primaryDomain": "Recovery & Readiness",
 "domains": ["Recovery & Readiness", "Training & Performance"],
 "audiences": ["Performance", "Athletic Training", "Nutrition"],
 "sports": ["Soccer"],
 "populations": ["Professional / Elite", "Male Athletes", "Healthy Athletes"],
 "evidenceSummary": "Randomized parallel-group trial in 20 U-21 Mexican national team players, of whom 18 completed it (9 per group). After an unofficial game and the following day, players received either a carbohydrate-protein drink with foam rolling, cold-water immersion and tart cherry juice, or a carbohydrate-protein drink with stretching and intermittent cold-water immersion. Both protocols showed recovery over time, with creatine kinase back to baseline by 68 hours and jump and strength measures back near baseline by 44 hours, and no between-protocol main effect was found.",
 "screeningLimitations": "There was no control group, so the trial cannot show that either protocol beats no intervention, and 9 players per arm gives low power to detect group differences. Players were male, from one national squad, and the game was unofficial; the CK to game-load correlations were secondary and exploratory.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff may read 'equally effective' as proof that either protocol speeds recovery, when the study had no control group and no between-protocol difference.",
 "paper": {
  "year": 2023,
  "citation": "Altarriba-Bartes A, Vicens-Bordas J, Peña J, Alarcón-Palacios F, Sixtos-Meliton LA, Matabosch-Pijuan M, et al. The effectiveness of two comprehensive recovery protocols on performance and physiological measures in elite soccer players: A parallel group-randomized trial. International Journal of Sports Science & Coaching. 2023:1-11.",
  "doi": "10.1177/17479541231155585",
  "abstract": "In a randomized parallel-group trial, 18 U-21 Mexican national team players received one of two post-game recovery protocols after an unofficial game. Both protocols were followed by changes over time in creatine kinase, jump height, hamstring strength and perceived recovery, and no significant difference was found between them.",
  "tldr": "Two different multi-part recovery packages after an unofficial game produced similar recovery over 68 hours in a small group of elite youth players. Neither was shown to be better, and there was no control group.",
  "methods": "Randomized parallel-group trial in 20 U-21 national team players, with 18 analysed (9 per group) after two withdrew due to in-game injuries. Protocol A combined a carbohydrate-protein drink, foam rolling, cold-water immersion and tart cherry juice; protocol B combined the drink, static stretching and intermittent cold-water immersion. Creatine kinase (CK-III), countermovement jump, hamstring maximal voluntary contraction, perceived recovery and soreness were measured before, immediately after, and 20, 44 and 68 hours after the game.",
  "findings": "Both protocols showed a significant time effect for all outcomes (p below 0.001), with CK-III back to baseline by 68 hours and neuromuscular and perceptual outcomes back near baseline by 44 hours. No main effect of protocol was found. Group-by-time interactions were significant for countermovement jump (p = 0.035), non-dominant hamstring strength (p = 0.036) and perceived recovery (p = 0.01), with the changes mainly in the foam-roller group. CK-III change correlated with accelerations, decelerations, high-speed running and sprint distance in the game (large to very large), but not with total distance.",
  "limitations": "There was no control group and only 9 players per arm, so non-significant group differences may reflect low power. The abstract says soreness changed in one group, but Table 1 shows no significant interaction for soreness (p = 0.34), and the abstract's claim that protocol A altered soreness is not supported; the countermovement jump drop of 3.2 cm at 20 hours in the foam-roller group was not statistically different from the other group.",
  "practicalImplications": "After games, staff can use either protocol, since neither was clearly better in this trial, and the authors suggest letting players choose based on preference and perceived effectiveness. Monitoring accelerations, decelerations and high-speed running alongside CK may help guide recovery decisions, though this was a secondary finding.",
  "athleteDev": "Both protocols were followed by a return of jump height and hamstring strength within 44 to 68 hours, so either can fit a squad's routine. The 3.2 cm jump drop at 20 hours in the foam-roller group was not a significant difference, so it should not be read as a reliable effect.",
  "rtp": "The study measured recovery in healthy players after an unofficial game, not after injury. It cannot inform return-to-sport decisions or show that either protocol speeds recovery from a hamstring or other injury."
 }
}

{
 "id": "Q23",
 "sourceFile": "Validity of research based on publicly obtained data in sports medicine - A quantitative assessment of concussions in the National Football League.pdf",
 "decision": "INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason": "",
 "degradedReason": "",
 "doiMissing": false,
 "identityCheck": "Title in the text (Validity of Research Based on Publicly Obtained Data in Sports Medicine: A Quantitative Assessment of Concussions in the National Football League) matches the filename, which is truncated.",
 "confidence": "high",
 "studyDesign": "Systematic Review / Meta-analysis",
 "primaryDomain": "Sports Medicine & Injury",
 "domains": ["Sports Medicine & Injury", "Brain Health & Psychology"],
 "audiences": ["Sports Medicine", "Research & Analytics", "Athletic Training"],
 "sports": ["American Football"],
 "populations": ["Professional / Elite", "Injured Athletes"],
 "evidenceSummary": "PRISMA systematic review of 20 concussion studies in NFL players that used publicly obtained internet data, searched to November 2020. Twelve studies with comparable data were checked against the NFL's electronic health record injury database for 2015 to 2019. On average the public-data studies captured 70% of the database's concussions (range 20.1% to 90.2%), over-represented running backs and quarterbacks, and under-counted special teams plays.",
 "screeningLimitations": "The reference standard is the NFL's own injury database, and two authors are NFL staff or consultants, so the reference is not independently validated. Study periods in the comparison table (mostly 2012 to 2015) do not match the 2015 to 2019 NFL average used for the comparison, and most included studies had low quality scores.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could read the 70% capture figure as the true rate of NFL concussions, or conclude that every study built on public data is unreliable; the paper is a validity check on one group of studies and does not measure concussion incidence.",
 "paper": {
  "year": 2023,
  "citation": "Inclan PM, Kuhn AW, Chang PS, Mack C, Solomon GS, Sills AK, et al. Validity of Research Based on Publicly Obtained Data in Sports Medicine: A Quantitative Assessment of Concussions in the National Football League. Sports Health. 2023.",
  "doi": "10.1177/19417381231167333",
  "abstract": "A systematic review of 20 concussion studies that used publicly sourced data on NFL players was compared with the NFL's electronic health record injury database. The public-data studies captured about 70% of the concussions in the league database on average, with wide variation and a bias toward high-profile positions.",
  "tldr": "Studies built on public internet sources captured about 70% of NFL concussions on average, with individual studies ranging from 20% to 90%. Treat their position and special teams findings with particular caution.",
  "methods": "PRISMA systematic review of studies using publicly obtained NFL concussion data, searched in November 2020, with duplicate screening by two reviewers. Twelve studies with comparable data were checked against NFL injury database counts for 2015 to 2019, and capture rates, game phase and position distributions were compared. Study quality was scored with the MINORS tool.",
  "findings": "Public-data studies captured 70.0% (SD 25.0%) of database concussions, with a range of 20.1% to 90.2%. They reported more concussions on offense (55% vs 44%) and far fewer on special teams (under 1% vs 18%). Running backs and quarterbacks were over-represented, while offensive linemen, defensive backs and linebackers were under-represented. Excluding the two lowest-capturing studies raised the average by about 10 percentage points.",
  "limitations": "The reference database is the NFL's own system and two authors are NFL-affiliated, and the comparison periods of several public-data studies do not match the 2015 to 2019 average. The included studies had generally low quality scores (average 9.8 for non-comparative studies), and the 'meta-analysis' label in the flow diagram refers only to pooled averages.",
  "practicalImplications": "Researchers and staff should not use publicly sourced concussion data as a stand-in for medical records, especially for position-level or special teams claims. Where such data are used, report the capture rate and known biases, and prefer curated databases linked to medical records.",
  "athleteDev": "This is not a performance paper. For performance or workload analysis built on public game data, the paper warns that such sources can miss injuries and misassign positions, which can distort conclusions about which players are at risk.",
  "rtp": "The paper does not report return-to-play results for any player, so it cannot guide return-to-play decisions or safety timelines. It only checks how completely public sources recorded concussions."
 }
}
